01

Executive summary

Come Together is an unofficial, personal kinetic-typography lyric video set to The Beatles' 1969 track, a design exercise in syncing motion to music, not an authorised Beatles release.

The brief I set myself was about intersection: syncing visual elements to musical rhythm so the typography and imagery amplify the song's emotional register rather than just illustrating it literally. I want to be clear upfront that I'm not reproducing the song's lyrics anywhere in this write-up: the lyric-timing work described below is about the animation technique, not the words themselves, and this piece is a personal design exercise rather than commissioned or licensed work.

02

Background

This project sat alongside two other motion graphics pieces built during the same module. It was where the Cinema 4D to After Effects pipeline via Cineware and character-animation certification (After Effects CC 2021 Character Animation Essential Training) got their most direct application, driving both the four band-member figures and the closing Volkswagen van sequence.

03

The brief

Reimagine The Beatles' "Come Together" as a motion graphics lyric video that pairs the song's late-1960s cultural moment with contemporary kinetic typography and 3D animation, without losing the track's own visual identity.

04

Brand system

The visual identity leans directly on the Abbey Road album cover itself: a vivid mustard-amber backdrop standing in for the golden-age rock and roll register, with four silhouetted figures, each individually styled to reflect a distinct band member's silhouette, striding across the frame in a monochromatic treatment. The band's name sits across the figures in bold white lettering, positioned so the members' silhouettes and the letterforms visually interlock rather than sitting as separate layers.

Typography runs across Bebas Neue Pro, a SemiExpanded Bold cut, and an Expanded ExtraBold cut: all condensed, high-impact display faces suited to lyrics that need to read fast and land hard in a short on-screen window. The colour palette pulls warm coral, earthy mustard, golden ochre and dark gold against classic onyx and deep charcoal, keeping the whole thing tonally inside that Abbey Road amber-and-black register rather than introducing colours the reference doesn't support.

05

Storyboard

Storyboarding here meant breaking the track into its actual musical beats and phrases first, then building visuals that harmonised with each section's mood rather than working scene-by-scene in the abstract. The panels track a clear arc: a single figure, then figures accumulating into the full group, walking sequences building toward the Abbey Road crossing itself, rendered from both street level and overhead, before the closing sequence shifts to a Volkswagen camper van driving into a sunset, a visual coda that isn't literally in the album artwork but extends its road-trip, free-spirited tone.

06

Production pipeline: Cinema 4D & After Effects integration

The four band-member figures were modelled and assembled in Cinema 4D, then brought into After Effects with a Two-Node Camera setup via Maxon's Cineware plugin: the bridge that let the 3D camera and the 2D compositing work stay in sync rather than being reconciled after the fact. PBR lighting was applied to the figures specifically to make them read correctly once composited against the flat amber background, and the camera was choreographed to rotate and move around the group with eased keyframes rather than a static or linear pan. The band logo went through its own revision here too: it initially blended too closely with the figures against the amber background, so I changed it to white specifically to hold its own depth and contrast.

07

Production pipeline: animation & composition

Typography animation ran in five passes, moving from a simple loop-timed opening line synced to the track's intro, through lyric placeholders positioned next to each band member's face, then a version where the camera itself pushes forward into the figures as lyrics arrive, giving the typography a sense of arriving in three-dimensional space rather than sitting flat on a 2D plane. The zebra crossing itself (the single most recognisable visual element of the reference) was built as its own asset specifically to anchor the Abbey Road homage once the camera rotated overhead, with the final typography pass placing lyric text over the crossing sequence as the band's silhouettes complete the walk.

08

Production pipeline: the VW van

A second 3D thread ran alongside the band figures: a Volkswagen camper van, imported and textured in Cinema 4D with a period-appropriate paint treatment, animated with independent front and rear wheel movement, including keyframed wobble on the rear tyres specifically to sell the sense of the van actually being in motion rather than sliding across a flat plane. The band's logo was placed on the van's side and, in a later pass, on the rear as it drives away from camera, a small continuity choice that keeps the brand element present even as the composition's focus shifts to the van itself.

The closing sequence builds a full sunset backdrop behind the van, with the camera panning from a high angle down to road level to track the vehicle heading toward the horizon, and animated road lines reinforcing the sense of forward travel as the piece closes.

09

Sound

The final piece is set to the official 2019 remix and remaster of Come Together from Abbey Road (Super Deluxe Edition), the real, licensed recording, sourced and referenced via Apple Music rather than a cover or recreation. That's a meaningful distinction to make plainly: this is a fan-made, unofficial visual accompaniment to an existing commercial recording, not a piece using original music, and it's presented here as a design and animation exercise rather than as something intended for public release or monetisation.

10

Reflection

This project was the clearest test of the Cinema 4D to After Effects pipeline across the whole module: two separate 3D threads (the band figures, the VW van) both needing to composite cleanly against the same flat amber background without looking like they belonged to different pieces.

Working with the Abbey Road cover's own composition, rather than inventing an unrelated visual treatment, is the decision I'd defend most confidently: the zebra crossing and the four-silhouette arrangement do more to signal "Beatles" instantly than any amount of original design work could.

11

Lessons learned

Cineware's Two-Node Camera setup is what actually made the 3D-to-2D handoff work: trying to reconcile a separately-animated 3D camera with 2D compositing after the fact would have meant constant re-work. Setting that bridge up correctly at the start of the project, rather than partway through, saved real time later.

13

Interview story

Situation

My motion graphics module required a piece demonstrating kinetic typography synced tightly to music, alongside 3D character and vehicle animation.

Task

Build a lyric video for an existing, iconic song that felt genuinely synced to the music rather than illustrated over the top of it, while respecting the track's own visual identity.

Action

I modelled four band-member figures in Cinema 4D, brought them into After Effects via Cineware with a synced camera rig, and built five passes of typography animation moving from simple loops to full camera-driven lyric reveals. A second 3D thread (a fully textured and animated VW van) extended the piece's visual language into its closing sequence.

Result

A complete kinetic-typography piece with two integrated 3D animation threads, set to the track's own official recording, and a clear understanding of how to build a Cinema 4D to After Effects camera pipeline that doesn't require constant reconciliation between the two halves.
